theme_scores.justification: The manifesto commitment and claim about three-quarters of apprentices working in the private sector are asserted without any underlying data, study, or citation explaining their basis.

theme_scores.theme: Diversity and Inclusion in the Workforce
theme_scores.justification: The statement that '15% of people who have autism currently in full time employment' is a specific figure used to support the diagnosis of a diversity challenge, but it carries no citation or reference.

reasoning: Neither core theme provides evidence that reaches level 2. In 'Apprenticeship Policy and Economic Growth', the claims about the manifesto target and the private-sector apprenticeship proportion ('an estimated three-quarters of apprentices work') are presented as background assertions rather than evidence supporting a diagnosis of skills shortages; no figures, studies, or sources are given to substantiate the existence or scale of the skills shortage itself. In 'Diversity and Inclusion in the Workforce', the sentence 'only 15% of people who have autism currently in full time employment' does offer a concrete statistic used to support the claim that diversity/inclusion is a significant challenge, reaching level 1 — but it has no reference or link, so it cannot reach level 2. No theme assesses the strengths, weaknesses, or uncertainties of any evidence, so level 3 is out of reach entirely. Because the core theme on apprenticeships and growth — which carries much of the diagnostic weight about skills shortages — has no evidence at all, and the other core theme reaches only level 1 with an uncited statistic, the section as a whole cannot be judged higher than level 1. A stronger document would cite the source for the 15% autism employment figure and provide data (e.g., skills gap surveys, apprenticeship outcome studies) underpinning the manifesto target and the three-quarters figure, linking each explicitly to the stated problem.
